summary:
I've been building The Long Rest, a D&D campaign manager, and most of the recent work has been fixing bugs that only show up once real people play with it. The video call feature shipped with nobody able to hear each other — turned out LiveKit was subscribing to remote audio tracks but nothing ever attached them to a media element to actually play the sound. Fixed it, then built a two-browser test harness (headless Chrome over a debugging protocol, fake audio devices) so I could prove audio worked end to end without needing prod credentials.

The AI assistant (the "Oracle") had a grounding problem: it told a player a paladin's subclass ability was "a reaction spell," which was just wrong, then admitted it had guessed. I traced it to four separate causes stacked on top of each other — the system prompt claimed we had the full rulebooks when we only had the open-license core rules, the fallback logic explicitly permitted guessing when nothing was found, one global temperature setting applied to a factual rules lookup, and the character importer was silently dropping subclass features so the AI didn't even know the character had that ability. Fixing all four took the answer from confidently wrong to "I don't have that text — here's which subclass has it, which book should I check."

I also found a real privacy leak in the notes system: editing a DM-only journal entry silently re-published it to the whole party, because the re-indexing code rebuilt the search chunks without preserving the "DM-only" flag — a missing flag was being read as "visible to everyone." Traced it, confirmed it live with a throwaway test document, shipped a fix, and ran a backfill to correct anything already affected.

Alongside that I built out a note-tagging system so a single session-prep document can mark which parts are for players, which are DM secrets, and which are "reveal later" — with the rule that anything unmarked defaults to hidden, since the wrong failure mode here is a spoiler, not a locked door.
